a: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good;
t: Book Five opens with the temple's refrain
p: The same call opens Psalms 106, 118 and 136, and the Chronicler puts it in the Levites' mouths.
b: Psalm 107 begins the fifth and last book of the Psalter (Psalms 107–150). Its first line was a refrain of temple worship: "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; / his loyal love is forever" (1 Chronicles 16:34). The Chronicler has the Levite singers use it when the ark comes to Jerusalem, at the temple's dedication (2 Chronicles 5:13; 7:3) and on the march against Moab and Ammon (2 Chronicles 20:21), and the returned exiles sing it when the second temple's foundation is laid (Ezra 3:11). Jeremiah expects it to be heard again in Jerusalem's empty streets (Jeremiah 33:11). It frames Psalm 118 and runs through all of Psalm 136.
r: 106:1; 118:1; 118:29; 136:1; 1 Chronicles 16:34; 2 Chronicles 5:13; 2 Chronicles 7:3; 2 Chronicles 20:21; Ezra 3:11; Jeremiah 33:11

a: his loyal love is forever
p: Book Four ends with a plea to be gathered from the nations; Book Five opens with the gathered giving thanks.
b: Psalm 106 ends Book Four with the prayer "Gather us and pull us out from the nations" (106:47; the same words are in 1 Chronicles 16:35). Psalm 107 opens Book Five with people the LORD has been "gathering them from the lands" (107:3). The editors of the Psalter seem to have placed the two side by side on purpose: the plea of the exiles, then the thanks of those who came home. Gerald Wilson argued that Book Five as a whole answers the crisis of exile and the loss of David's throne lamented at the end of Book Three (89:38–51) with praise of God as king.

a: Let those the LORD has redeemed say it,
p: A go'el buys back a relative. Isaiah calls the exiles coming home "the LORD's redeemed".
b: Ga'al is what a family redeemer does: he buys back land or a relative lost to debt (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4:4). When God is the redeemer, the picture is of a kinsman paying to get his own people back. "The redeemed of the LORD" is a phrase from Isaiah's prophecies of return (Isaiah 62:12; compare Isaiah 35:10 and Isaiah 51:11, which have "ransomed"). Verses 2–3 sound the same note: these people have been gathered from the lands. The four stories that follow may describe the exiles' own experiences, or simply the many ways God saves people in trouble.

a: from the north and from the sea
p: "The sea" usually means the west, which is already named. Many think "the south" was meant.
b: The four directions should be east, west, north and south, but the Hebrew ends "and from the sea". In Israel "the sea", the Mediterranean, usually stands for the west, and the west is already in the list. Some take "the sea" here as the Red Sea to the south, or as the coastlands beyond the sea (Isaiah 49:12 has a similar list with a "sea" in it). Others change one letter to read yamin, "the right hand", which in Hebrew is the south (89:12). The Greek also has "sea". The Qumran scroll 4QPs-f (4Q88) is broken here, but its last surviving letter is probably a final mem, which fits yam, "sea", and not yamin. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: They strayed in the wilderness, on a wasteland road;
p: Lost travelers, prisoners, the sick and sailors: four scenes with one refrain.
b: Verses 4–32 tell four short stories: travelers lost in the desert (107:4–9), prisoners in the dark (107:10–16), fools sick near death (107:17–22) and sailors in a storm (107:23–32). Each follows the same steps: trouble, a cry to the LORD, rescue, and a call to give thanks, held together by two refrains (107:6, 13, 19, 28 and 107:8, 15, 21, 31). Some scholars picture four groups bringing thank offerings at a festival, each with its own story. Others read the scenes as pictures of Israel's exile and return: wandering, captivity, sickness for sin, the sea. The last part (107:33–43) changes into a hymn about how God turns lands and fortunes around.

a: hemmed in as they were
p: Trouble in Hebrew is a narrow place; rescue is open space.
b: Tsar is a tight, narrow place, and metsuqot, "troubles", comes from a verb meaning to press hard. Hebrew pictures distress as being squeezed and rescue as room to breathe: "From the narrow place I called on Yah; / Yah answered me and set me in the open" (118:5; compare 4:1; 18:19). The Plain keeps the picture with "hemmed in" and "tight places". The refrain comes back four times with a different verb each time: he "pulled them free" (107:6), "saved them" (107:13, 19), "brought them" out (107:28).

a: Let them give the LORD thanks for his loyal love,
p: To "give thanks" (hodah) is to tell in front of others what God has done.
b: The verb hodah means to acknowledge or confess. Thanks in Israel was not only a private feeling but a public report: the rescued person tells the story at the temple, often over a thank offering (107:22; 116:14, 17), so that others hear what God did. That is why the refrain adds "for human beings": God's loyal love is on display for everyone. The noun todah means both "thanks" and the thank offering itself (Leviticus 7:12; 50:14). For hesed, "loyal love", see the topic page.

a: For he has given the craving soul its fill,
p: Nefesh is first the throat or appetite, then the life and the self. Mary's song echoes this verse.
b: Nefesh is often translated "soul", but its basic sense is the throat, the part that hungers and thirsts, and from there the appetite, the life, and the whole living self. In this psalm the word keeps that bodily feel: life fading out in the hungry (107:5), a craving soul and a hungry soul (107:9), throats that turn from food (107:18), nerve melting in fear (107:26). Mary's song says of God, "The hungry he has loaded with good things" (Luke 1:53), close to the Greek of this verse.

a: deep shadow
t: Deep shadow, or the shadow of death
p: Tsalmavet was read "shadow of death"; most now take it as "deep darkness".
b: The Masoretic vowels divide the word as tsal-mavet, "shadow of death", and so did the Greek (skia thanatou) and the KJV. Most scholars think it is one noun from a root meaning "to be dark", "deep darkness". This site renders it "deep shadow" (as in 23:4), and a dark prison fits either sense. Isaiah uses the same pictures for captives whom God will free (Isaiah 9:2; Isaiah 42:7), and Zechariah's song speaks of "people sitting in the dark, in death's shadow" (Luke 1:79).

a: because they had rebelled against God's words
p: The prisoners are there for their own rebellion, as Judah went into exile for its sins; yet they are rescued.
b: The second and third stories say plainly that the trouble came from sin: the prisoners "rebelled against God's words", and the fools suffered "for their rebel ways" (107:17). Readers after the exile would hear their own history: the prophets had warned that Judah would go into captivity for refusing God's counsel (2 Kings 17:13–14; Jeremiah 25:4–11). The psalm does not stop at guilt. The same people cry out and are rescued, and they too are called to give thanks. Isaiah uses these images for the coming release of captives (Isaiah 42:7; Isaiah 61:1), and Luke has Jesus read Isaiah 61 in the Nazareth synagogue (Luke 4:18).

a: For he has broken bronze gates to pieces
p: Isaiah has God promise Cyrus the same thing: bronze doors broken, iron bars cut through.
b: Isaiah 45:2 uses the same pair of images in God's promise to Cyrus, the Persian king who would free the exiles: bronze doors broken, iron bars cut through. Babylon's gates were famous; Herodotus says its wall had a hundred gates, all of bronze (Histories 1.179). Whether the psalm borrows from Isaiah or not, its first readers would have heard the fall of Babylon in it. Christian writers later used the line for Christ breaking the gates of death and freeing the dead.

a: Fools they were
p: Many scholars change "fools" to "sick people". No Hebrew manuscript has that, and the Greek differs again.
b: The Hebrew says "fools", the word Proverbs uses for people who scorn wisdom and correction (Proverbs 1:7). The story that follows is about sickness: they cannot eat and come near death. So many scholars change ʾevilim to cholim, "sick people", and some modern versions print that. No Hebrew manuscript has it. The Greek has another reading: "He took hold of them out of their lawless way." The Plain keeps "fools": in the wisdom books, folly and sin can make a person ill (Proverbs 3:7–8; Psalm 38:3–5).

a: the gates of death
p: Death is pictured as a city with gates, as in 9:13 and in Jesus' words about "the gates of Hades".
b: The dead were pictured as gathered in a walled city under the earth, Sheol, with gates that shut behind them (Job 38:17; Isaiah 38:10). To "reach the gates of death" is to be at the point of dying, and to be lifted "from the gates of death" is to be healed (9:13). Jesus' promise that "the gates of Hades" will not overpower his church uses the same picture (Matthew 16:18).

a: He sent his word to heal them
p: God's word acts like a messenger. Church fathers heard Christ, the Word, in this line.
b: God's word here is almost a person: he "sends" it, and it heals and rescues (compare 147:15, 18; Isaiah 55:11). In the psalm it is God's command of healing. The Wisdom of Solomon says the Israelites bitten by snakes in the wilderness were healed not by any herb or ointment but by God's word (Wisdom of Solomon 16:12). Church fathers such as Augustine read the line of Christ, the Word who became flesh (John 1:14). A centurion's request to Jesus, "Only say a word, and my servant will get well" (Matthew 8:8), shows the same trust in a word that heals.
r: 147:15; 147:18; Isaiah 55:11; Wisdom of Solomon 16:12; John 1:14; Matthew 8:8

a: Let them sacrifice thank offerings
p: A thank offering was a peace offering eaten in a meal with family and friends on the day it was given.
b: The zevach todah was a kind of peace offering. Part went to the altar, part to the priest, and the rest was eaten by the worshiper and his guests that same day, with loaves of bread (Leviticus 7:11–15). So a rescue was celebrated with a feast and a story. 50:14 and 50:23 prefer it to other sacrifices, and 116:17 brings one. The rabbis said that in the age to come all sacrifices will cease except the thank offering (Leviticus Rabbah 9:7).

a: Others took ships down to the sea
p: Masoretic manuscripts set a strange reversed letter after 107:20–27 and before 107:40.
b: In the Leningrad Codex and other Masoretic manuscripts, a mark shaped like a reversed letter nun stands after each of 107:20–27 and after 107:39, just before 107:40; the manuscripts do not all place the marks alike. The same mark brackets Numbers 10:35–36. The Talmud says these verses have such signs because they are "exceptions" (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 17b). Scholars think the marks flag verses that a scribe thought out of place. Nothing in the wording is in doubt, and every witness has the verses.

a: and traded on the wide waters
p: Israel had little sea trade of its own; the sea was strange and dangerous to most Israelites.
b: Israel had few good harbors. Solomon's ships sailed with Phoenician crews, and Jehoshaphat's fleet was wrecked before it left port (1 Kings 9:26–28; 1 Kings 22:48). For most Israelites the sea was a picture of chaos that only God controls (89:9; 93:3–4). Jonah's storm follows the same steps as this story: a storm sent by God, terrified sailors, prayer, a sudden calm (Jonah 1:4–16).

a: and all their skill was swallowed up
p: Chokhmah is skill as well as wisdom: the sailors' know-how is gulped down by the sea.
b: Chokhmah is the usual word for "wisdom", but it often means practical skill, the craft of a weaver or builder (Exodus 35:31–35). Here it is seamanship. The verb pictures the sea swallowing it, as the earth "swallowed" Pharaoh's army (Exodus 15:12). The old English "at their wits' end" (KJV) catches the sense. The experts have nothing left but a cry to the LORD.

a: He brought the gale down to a hush
p: The Gospels tell of Jesus calming a storm in a way that points back to this psalm.
b: In a storm on the Sea of Galilee, Jesus' terrified disciples wake him; he rebukes the wind, and there is "a great calm". They ask one another who this can be, when wind and sea do what he says (Mark 4:39–41; Matthew 8:23–27; Luke 8:22–25). Readers who knew Psalm 107 knew where the question points: in the psalm it is the LORD who raises the storm and brings it down to a hush. Jonah's storm also ends with the sea growing still (Jonah 1:15).

a: the port they longed for
p: Machoz appears only here. It matches an Akkadian word for a town or market.
b: Machoz occurs only here in the Bible. It matches the Akkadian māḫāzu, "town, market place", and in later Aramaic it is used for a harbor town. So the traders of 107:23 are brought to the port they wanted. The KJV's "their desired haven" is the source of an English phrase still used today.

a: where the elders sit
p: The rescued tell their story in the people's assembly and before the elders at the gate.
b: "The gathering of the people" and "where the elders sit" are the two places of public life: the worship assembly and the council of older men who judged cases at the town gate (Ruth 4:1–2; Proverbs 31:23). Thanks belongs where the whole community can hear it.

a: He makes rivers into wilderness
p: The closing hymn reverses fortunes, as Hannah's song, Isaiah and Mary's song do.
b: Verses 33–41 change from story to hymn. God turns rivers into desert and desert into springs, sends nobles wandering and lifts the needy. The salt land (107:34) recalls the ruin of Sodom and the Dead Sea plain (Genesis 19:24–26; Deuteronomy 29:23). Desert turned to pools is one of Isaiah's pictures of the return from exile (Isaiah 35:6–7; Isaiah 41:18). "He brings low, he lifts up" is the theme of Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:4–8) and of Psalm 113, and it comes back in Mary's song (Luke 1:51–53).
r: Genesis 19:24–26; Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 35:6–7; Isaiah 41:18; 1 Samuel 2:4–8; 113:7–9; Luke 1:51–53

a: He pours scorn on the nobles
p: This verse is two half-lines of Job 12 word for word, and 107:42 echoes Job too.
b: 107:40 joins Job 12:21a and Job 12:24b in exactly the same Hebrew, and 107:42 combines Job 22:19 and Job 5:16. The Plain uses the site's wording of Job for these lines. Either the psalm draws on Job, or both draw on a stock of wisdom sayings. In Job the words are bitter: God ruins leaders and no one can stop him. In the psalm they are praise: God humbles the proud and lifts the needy (107:41).

a: Who is wise? Let him take note of these things,
p: The last verse echoes the last verse of Hosea and turns the psalm into a lesson.
b: Hosea's book ends, "Who is wise enough to understand these things?" (Hosea 14:9). Psalm 107 ends the same way: the stories are for study as well as song. The plural "acts of loyal love" (chasdei YHWH) sums up the four rescues and the hymn. The wise will see God's hesed in the turns of history and of their own lives.

a: A song. A psalm of David.
p: In Hebrew Bibles 108:1 here is 108:2. The Greek and Latin give Psalms 107–118 other numbers.
b: This site numbers verses as English Bibles do: a psalm's title is verse 0. Hebrew Bibles count the title as verse 1, so in Psalm 108 every verse is one higher there (108:1 here is Hebrew 108:2). In Psalms 109 and 110 the short title is joined to the first line, and the numbers agree. The psalms themselves are numbered differently in the Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus) and the Latin Vulgate, which older Catholic Bibles and the Orthodox churches use: Psalms 107–113 are Greek 106–112; Psalms 114 and 115 together are Greek 113; Psalm 116 is Greek 114 (116:1–9) and 115 (116:10–19); Psalms 117 and 118 are Greek 116 and 117.

a: My heart is firm, God.
t: Two old psalms made into a new one
p: Psalm 108 joins 57:7–11 and 60:5–12 and leaves out the laments that opened both.
b: Verses 1–5 are 57:7–11 and verses 6–13 are 60:5–12, with small changes. The Plain uses the site's wording of those passages wherever the Hebrew is the same. What is left out matters: Psalm 57 began among lions and hunters, and Psalm 60 began "You have thrown us off, God." Psalm 108 keeps the confident praise and God's promise of the land, then the plea for help. Most scholars think the joining was done after the exile, when Edom (108:9–10) held land in southern Judah and was hated for joining in Jerusalem's fall (137:7; Obadiah 10–14). Both originals belong to the "Elohistic Psalter" (Psalms 42–83), which prefers "God" to "the LORD"; Psalm 108 has "LORD" in 108:3, where 57:9 has "Lord".

a: and my glory too
p: Psalm 57 said "Wake up, my glory!" Here "my glory" joins the singing.
b: In 57:8 the singer tells his kavod, his "glory", to wake up. Psalm 108 moves the word into its first verse: "I will sing; I will play music, and my glory too", or "yes, with my glory". See the note on 57:8 for what "glory" means there, probably the singer's whole self (compare 16:9; 30:12). The Greek has "in my glory".

a: and I will make music to you among the nations.
t: "Among the nations" written as two words
p: The Leningrad Codex writes the word as bal-ummim, as in 44:14, 57:9 and 149:7. The sense is not in doubt.
b: The Masoretic writing divides bal'ummim, "among the nations", into bal-ummim, which taken by itself would look like "not peoples". The Leningrad Codex writes it this way in all four places where it occurs (44:14; 57:9; 108:3; 149:7), so it is a fixed Masoretic writing, not a slip in one copy. Every ancient translation and the parallel first line, "among the peoples", show that the meaning is "among the nations".

a: higher than the heavens
p: 57:10 says God's love is as high as the heavens; 108:4 says it goes higher.
b: The one change in this verse is small. 57:10 has 'ad-shamayim, "up to the heavens"; 108:4 has me'al-shamayim, "above the heavens". The later psalm has God's loyal love outrun even the sky, which matches the next line, where God is asked to rise "over the heavens" (108:5).

a: God spoke in his holiness:
p: See the notes on 60:6–8 for Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Ephraim, Judah, Moab, Edom and Philistia.
b: The oracle in 108:7–9 repeats 60:6–8: God, as warrior and owner of the land, divides it up and claims both the tribes and the neighboring nations. For the places and images see the notes there. In Psalm 60 the oracle answered a lament over defeat; in Psalm 108 it follows praise, so it reads as a promise still waiting to be kept. Readers after the exile, living in a small province with Edom on its southern border, could pray it as a claim that the whole land, on both sides of the Jordan, still belonged to God.

a: Over Philistia I raise the war cry.
p: 60:8 reads "Shout over me, Philistia!" 108:9 makes God the one who shouts.
b: 60:8 has 'alay peleshet hitro'a'i, "over me, Philistia, shout!", which may be mocking ("go on, shout") or a call to Philistia to cheer its new master. 108:9 has 'alei-feleshet etro'a', "over Philistia I will shout": a victory cry, with God as the one who shouts. A scribe may have smoothed a hard line, or the change was deliberate. Teru'ah is an army's war shout (Joshua 6:5; 1 Samuel 17:20). The Greek has a different reading; see the variant.

a: the fortified city
p: 60:9 and 108:10 differ by one Hebrew word; both mean a fortified city. Edom's strongholds were Bozrah and Sela.
b: 60:9 has 'ir matsor, "city of siege", a walled city; 108:10 has 'ir mivtsar, "city of fortification". The two mean the same, and the Plain has "fortified city" in both. Edom's chief strongholds sat high in the mountains southeast of the Dead Sea: Bozrah (Isaiah 34:6; Isaiah 63:1) and the rock city Sela (2 Kings 14:7; Obadiah 3).

a: Have you not thrown us off, God?
p: 60:10 says "Is it not you, God...?"; 108:11 drops "you", and the complaint comes without the lament that led to it.
b: 60:10 has halo-attah Elohim, "Is it not you, God, who...?" Psalm 108 drops attah, "you". The sense is close. But in Psalm 108 the complaint about defeat comes without the long lament that made it natural in Psalm 60, so it reads as a sudden admission: the God who promised the land has let his people lose. The psalm still ends in trust (108:13).

a: O God, the one I praise,
p: The prayer opens and closes with praise (109:30), around the harshest curses in the Psalter.
b: Literally "God of my praise": the God the singer praises, or the God who gives him reason to praise (Deuteronomy 10:21). The prayer begins with praise and asks God not to stay silent while liars talk; it ends with the singer praising God among many people (109:30–31). Between them stands the longest string of curses in the Psalms (109:6–19).

a: they act as my accusers
p: The verb and noun satan run through the psalm: accusers in a court case.
b: Satan as a verb means to accuse or oppose; as a noun, an accuser or adversary, often in a court. Psalm 109 uses it four times: the enemies "act as my accusers" (109:4), "an accuser" (satan) is to stand at the wicked man's right hand (109:6), and "my accusers" (sotnai) appear in 109:20 and 109:29. The scene is a trial: false witnesses, a judge, a verdict (109:7, 31). See the note on 109:6.

a: and I? I am all prayer.
p: The Hebrew has no verb. The singer answers slander only with prayer.
b: The Hebrew is two words: "and I, prayer". Most take it to mean "I keep praying" or "I am a man of prayer". Some think it means "I prayed for them" (compare 35:13, where the singer prayed and fasted for men who later turned on him). Either way his only weapon is to bring the matter to God. Compare 120:7, "I am peace", with the same shape. The Greek reads "but I kept praying".

a: Set a wicked man over him;
p: Verses 6–19 switch to "him". Some read them as the enemies' curse on the singer, quoted in his prayer.
b: Verses 1–5 speak of many enemies ("they"); 109:6–19 curse one man ("him"); 109:20 goes back to "my accusers". (1) The traditional reading: the singer himself curses his chief enemy, as other psalms do (35:4–8; 69:22–28). Acts reads it this way and applies 109:8 to Judas (Acts 1:20). (2) Many recent scholars, Erich Zenger among them, take 109:6–19 as the accusers' words against the singer, which he quotes to God, and read 109:20 as "This is what my accusers do before the LORD." The Hebrew has no sign of a quotation, and both readings are possible. The Plain leaves the text as it stands.

a: an accuser
p: The KJV has "let Satan stand at his right hand". The Hebrew has no "the" and probably means a human accuser.
b: The KJV reads "let Satan stand at his right hand". In the Hebrew satan has no article and stands parallel to "a wicked man", so most translators take it as a human accuser: let a wicked man judge him, and a prosecutor stand ready. In court the accuser stood at the right hand of the accused, as "the Accuser" stands at the high priest's right in Zechariah 3:1. The Greek has diabolos, "slanderer", the word the New Testament uses for the devil, which helped later readers find the devil here. The psalm ends with God himself standing at the right hand of the needy (109:31).

a: may his very prayer turn into sin
t: A prayer that counts as sin
p: If his plea in court counts against him, he has no appeal left.
b: In the trial scene the convicted man's plea for mercy, to the judge or to God, is to "become sin", that is, to count against him. Proverbs says the prayer of someone who will not listen to the law is abhorrent (Proverbs 28:9). It is one of the hardest lines in the psalm: it shuts even God's door. Christians who pray the psalm have often applied it to Judas (see 109:8) or to evil itself rather than to any living person.

a: let another man take over his charge
p: Peter applies this line to Judas, "Let another take his position", and the apostles choose Matthias.
b: Before Pentecost, Peter tells the believers that Judas's place among the Twelve must be filled, and quotes two psalms in their Greek form: "Let his homestead become desolate, and let no one live in it" (69:25, in the Greek) and "Let another take his position" (109:8; Acts 1:20). The Hebrew pequddah means a charge, an office or post; the Greek has episkopē, "oversight", the word behind English "episcopal" and, through Latin, "bishop". For Luke the psalms that cried out against a treacherous friend describe what happened to Jesus' betrayer (compare 41:9; John 13:18), and the line about "another" authorizes choosing Matthias (Acts 1:21–26). Some church writers called Psalm 109 the psalm about Judas.

a: Let the moneylender set a trap for all he has,
p: A lender could seize land, goods and even children for unpaid debt.
b: Nosheh is a creditor. In Israel and its neighbors a lender could take a debtor's property, and even his children as slaves (2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:1–5). The law tried to limit this (Exodus 22:25–27; Deuteronomy 24:10–13). The curse asks that the oppressor suffer what he did to others: he "chased down the poor and the needy" (109:16).

a: Let his ancestors' guilt be kept in the LORD's memory,
p: The curse reaches back to the parents and forward to the children, a pattern Ezekiel later rejects.
b: The curses widen in both directions: the man's children are to beg and his line to end (109:9–13), and his parents' sins are to stay on record. In the ancient world a family stood or fell together, and the Ten Words speak of guilt carried to the third and fourth generation of those who hate God (Exodus 20:5). Ezekiel and Deuteronomy insist that each person dies for his own sin (Ezekiel 18:1–20; Deuteronomy 24:16). Readers have found this part of the psalm the hardest, and it is one reason some churches leave the psalm out of public worship (see the chapter page).

a: For he did not remember to show loyal love.
p: He showed no loyal love and hounded the poor to death, so the curse asks that no loyal love be shown to him.
b: The curse is not random. The enemy "did not remember to show loyal love" (hesed) and hunted the poor to their death, so the curse asks that no one show hesed to him (109:12). It follows the rule of measure for measure found in the law (Exodus 21:23–25; Deuteronomy 19:19). The singer calls himself "poor and needy" (109:22), so the case is personal, but his appeal is to a God who defends the poor (109:31; 140:12).

a: He wore cursing like his robe;
p: The curse he loved becomes his clothes, his drink and the oil in his bones.
b: The images move inward: cursing is first his robe and belt (109:18–19), then water running into his insides and oil soaking into his bones. A spoken curse was thought to work like a living thing once released (Zechariah 5:1–4). In the ordeal for a suspected wife, the "water of bitterness" entered the body (Numbers 5:22–24). The point is that he becomes what he loved. The singer's accusers will be clothed too, with shame (109:29; compare 35:26).

a: This is my accusers' pay from the LORD,
p: Pe'ullah means work or wages. The verse may be a wish, or a summary of what the accusers said.
b: Pe'ullah is a worker's pay (Leviticus 19:13) or simply what someone does. Read as "pay", the verse is a wish: let all this be my accusers' wages from the LORD. Read as "doing", it sums up 109:6–19 as the accusers' own work, the curse they spoke against the singer (see the note on 109:6). The Greek has "This is the work of those who slander me, from the Lord." The Plain keeps "pay", the usual reading of the Hebrew.

a: But you, LORD, my Lord,
p: The turn to God begins with an emphatic "but you" and two names of God.
b: After the curses the prayer turns with ve'attah, "but you". The singer names God twice, YHWH Adonai, as in 68:20 and 140:7. In the Leningrad Codex the divine name here carries the vowels of Elohim, the scribes' sign that a reader should not say "Adonai" twice in a row. Now he asks nothing about his enemies, only rescue "for the sake of your name": God's reputation is tied to keeping faith with the poor.

a: I am shaken out like a locust
p: Two pictures of frailty: an evening shadow about to vanish, a locust flicked off a robe.
b: A shadow "as it stretches out" is the long shadow just before sunset, about to vanish (102:11; 144:4). A locust that lands on a garment is shaken out with a flick (compare the locusts swept away by wind in Exodus 10:19). The singer feels that easily brushed out of life.

a: My knees buckle from fasting,
p: Fasting was a way to plead with God; it also left the body weak.
b: Israelites fasted in mourning and in urgent prayer (35:13; 2 Samuel 12:16; Joel 2:12). The singer has fasted so long that his knees give way. "With no fat on it" is literally "lean from fat" or "without oil": he has stopped eating, and perhaps stopped putting oil on his skin, as mourners did (2 Samuel 14:2).

a: they see me and toss their heads
p: The same gesture of scorn is made at Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:39; Mark 15:29).
b: Shaking or wagging the head is a gesture of mockery (22:7; Lamentations 2:15). Matthew and Mark tell that people passing the cross were insulting Jesus, "wagging their heads" (Matthew 27:39; Mark 15:29). Christians who read Psalm 109 as a prayer of Christ (see the chapter page) found the scene here as well as in Psalm 22.

a: They curse, and you bless.
p: God's blessing outweighs their curse, as Balaam learned. The New Testament turns this into a rule of life.
b: Whatever the enemies say, God's blessing is stronger. Balaam was hired to curse Israel and could only bless (Numbers 23:8; Deuteronomy 23:5). The New Testament turns the line into a way of life: "Bless the ones who curse you" (Luke 6:28); "Bless them, and never curse" (Romans 12:14). Some Christian readers find here the key to praying the psalm: the singer hands the curse over to God and keeps the blessing for himself.

a: For he takes his stand at the needy one's right hand,
p: In 109:6 an accuser stands at the wicked man's right; here God stands at the needy one's right, as his defender.
b: The psalm ends by reversing 109:6: God himself takes the place of the defender beside the poor man on trial, to save him from those who would pass sentence on him. The "right hand" runs on into the next psalm, where the king sits at God's right hand and "the Lord" is at the king's right (110:1, 5; compare 16:8; 121:5).

a: Of David. A psalm.
p: Jesus' argument assumes David speaks. Many scholars think a court prophet wrote it for a king of David's line.
b: The title says ledavid, "of David" or "for David". Jesus' question in the Gospels assumes that David is the speaker who calls someone else "my lord" (Mark 12:36–37), and Peter argues the same at Pentecost (Acts 2:34). Many scholars read the psalm as a prophet's oracle at the crowning of a king in Jerusalem, perhaps early in the monarchy; the title then means "for David" or "for David's line". A few have dated it as late as the Maccabean priest-kings of the 100s BC, but its old language and its picture of a Jerusalem king lead most to date it to the time of the kings.

a: The LORD declares
p: Ne'um YHWH is the prophets' formula: "the LORD's declaration". A prophet passes God's words to the king.
b: Ne'um YHWH, "the LORD's declaration", is the formula prophets use for a word received from God (Amos 2:11; Isaiah 1:24; Jeremiah 1:8); it appears only here in the Psalms. So the speaker of 110:1–4 claims to pass on God's own words to the king, as Nathan brought God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:4–17). David's last words are also called a ne'um, spoken by the Spirit of the LORD (2 Samuel 23:1–2), and the New Testament treats this psalm the same way: David spoke it "by the Holy Spirit" (Mark 12:36).

a: to my lord
p: The Hebrew vowels give adoni, a title for a human lord. Christian Bibles print "my Lord", after the New Testament.
b: The Masoretic vowels read la'doni, "to my lord", the ordinary polite title for a king, master or other superior (1 Samuel 25:24; 2 Samuel 14:9). When the Hebrew Bible means God, it has Adonai, with different vowels. The consonants alone could be read either way, and the Greek uses kyrios for both: "The Lord said to my lord." Christian Bibles usually print "my Lord", reading the psalm with Jesus' question about it (Mark 12:35–37). Jewish interpreters point out that the form adoni is not used for God, so the "lord" is a human figure: David, Abraham or the Messiah. The Plain prints "my lord" as the Hebrew vowels have it, without deciding who he is.

a: Sit at my right hand,
p: The New Testament quotes or echoes 110:1 more often than any other verse of the Old Testament.
b: Jesus asks how the Messiah can be David's son if David calls him "my lord" (Mark 12:35–37; Matthew 22:41–46; Luke 20:41–44). At his trial he tells the high priest, "you will see the Son of Man sitting at the Power's right hand and coming with the clouds of the sky" (Mark 14:62), joining this verse to Daniel 7:13. Peter argues at Pentecost that David did not go up to heaven, so the one told to sit is the risen Jesus (Acts 2:32–36). The line then becomes a basic Christian confession: Christ is seated at God's right hand (Romans 8:34; Ephesians 1:20; Colossians 3:1; Hebrews 1:3; Hebrews 1:13; Hebrews 8:1; Hebrews 10:12; Hebrews 12:2; 1 Peter 3:22), and the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds repeat it. David Hay counted some thirty quotations and allusions.
r: Mark 12:35–37; Mark 14:62; Daniel 7:13; Acts 2:32–36; Romans 8:34; Ephesians 1:20; Colossians 3:1; Hebrews 1:3; Hebrews 1:13; Hebrews 10:12; 1 Peter 3:22

a: as a stool for your feet
p: Kings were shown with conquered enemies under their feet; Tutankhamun's footstool is carved with bound foreigners.
b: A footstool went with a throne (Isaiah 66:1; 1 Chronicles 28:2). Egyptian and Assyrian art shows kings with their feet on defeated enemies (compare Joshua 10:24). A footstool from the tomb of Tutankhamun (about 1330 BC) is carved with bound foreign captives, so the king rested his feet on his enemies whenever he sat. Paul uses the line for Christ's reign until every power is put under his feet, the last enemy being death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

a: the scepter of your strength
p: God extends the king's rule from Zion. "Rule" (radah) is the word for mastery in Genesis 1:26.
b: The scepter (matteh, a staff or rod) is the sign of the king's power, like the "iron rod" of 2:9. God sends it out from Zion, the hill of the temple and palace (2:6). The command "Rule!" uses radah, to have dominion, the verb of Genesis 1:26–28 for humanity's rule over creation and of 72:8 for the king's rule "from sea to sea". The king rules "right among" his enemies: they are not gone yet, but he reigns anyway.

a: Your people are freewill offerings
t: The hardest verse in the Psalms?
p: Almost every word of 110:3 is disputed, and the Hebrew and Greek read it very differently.
b: Word by word the Hebrew says: "your people, freewill offerings, on the day of your strength (or army), in splendors of holiness, from the womb, from dawn, to you the dew of your youth." (1) The people give themselves freely, like a nedavah, a gift no one required (Exodus 35:29; Judges 5:2), on the day the king calls up his army (chayil). (2) "In holy splendor" may describe holy clothing, or (in many Hebrew manuscripts) "on the holy mountains". (3) "From the dawn's womb" (mishchar, a rare form of shachar, "dawn") pictures something born fresh at daybreak. (4) "The dew of your young years" may be the king's youthful strength renewed like morning dew, or his young warriors, as countless as dewdrops (2 Samuel 17:12). For the Greek reading, see the variants.

a: the dew of your young years is yours
t: "Before the morning star I fathered you"
p: The Greek reading made 110:3 a key text for Christ's eternal birth from the Father.
b: The Greek line "from the womb, before the morning star, I fathered you" links Psalm 110 to 2:7, "This day I have fathered you." Justin Martyr used it for Christ's birth from the Father before creation (Dialogue with Trypho 63; 76), and later fathers did the same; the Nicene Creed's "begotten of the Father before all ages" grew from readings like this. The Latin, ex utero ante luciferum genui te, is still sung as the Communion antiphon of the Christmas Mass during the Night. In the Hebrew the line is about the king's youth and strength. Jewish interpreters read it of David or of Abraham.

a: The LORD has taken an oath, and he will not go back on it:
t: An oath God will not take back
p: God's oath makes this priesthood permanent. Hebrews 7:20–22 makes much of it.
b: Nicham means to change one's mind or relent (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). God binds himself by oath, as he did to David (89:3; 89:35; 132:11). Hebrews argues that Levi's priests became priests without an oath, but this priest with one, so his priesthood is permanent and better (Hebrews 7:20–22).
orig: נִשְׁבַּע יְהוָה וְלֹא יִנָּחֵם (nishba' YHWH velo yinnachem)

a: You are a priest forever,
p: Genesis 14 has the only other Old Testament mention of Melchizedek: bread, wine, a blessing and a tithe.
b: In Genesis 14:18–20 "Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was a priest of God Most High." He blessed Abram, and Abram gave him a tenth of everything. Salem is Jerusalem (76:2). Psalm 110 makes the king of David's line, ruling in the same city, heir to that old priest-kingship. Israel's kings did sometimes act as priests: David wore the linen ephod, offered sacrifices and blessed the people (2 Samuel 6:13–18), and Solomon did the same at the temple's dedication (1 Kings 8:62–64). But the regular priesthood belonged to Aaron's family, and Uzziah was struck with skin disease for burning incense (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The psalm gives the king a priesthood of another kind, older than Aaron's.

a: a priest forever
p: Hebrews 5–7 builds its teaching on Christ as high priest on this one verse.
b: Hebrews quotes 110:4 again and again (Hebrews 5:6; Hebrews 5:10; Hebrews 6:20; Hebrews 7:17; Hebrews 7:21) and argues from it. (1) In Genesis Melchizedek has no recorded parents, birth or death, "without father, without mother, without genealogy", so he pictures a priest who lives forever (Hebrews 7:3). (2) Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing, so Melchizedek is greater than Abraham and than Levi, Abraham's descendant (Hebrews 7:4–10). (3) If God promised a priest of another order, Levi's priesthood was not final (Hebrews 7:11–19). (4) Jesus, from Judah and not Levi, is that priest, and because he lives forever his priesthood never passes to another (Hebrews 7:14; Hebrews 7:23–25).

a: after the pattern of Melchizedek
p: The phrase may mean "in the manner of Melchizedek", or "for my sake, a rightful king".
b: 'Al-divrat means "concerning" or "on account of" (Ecclesiastes 3:18; Ecclesiastes 8:2). With its old ending -i it is usually read "in the manner of": the king is a priest the way Melchizedek was, a king of Jerusalem who was also "priest of God Most High". The Greek has "according to the order (taxis) of Melchizedek", and Hebrews follows it. Some read the -i as "my" and take malki-tsedeq as words rather than a name: "by my word, a rightful king". The name itself means "my king is righteous" or "king of righteousness" (Hebrews 7:2). The Plain's "after the pattern" keeps the common sense.

a: Melchizedek
p: The Talmud says the priesthood passed from Melchizedek to Abraham; Qumran saw him as a heavenly judge.
b: The Talmud says God meant the priesthood to come from Melchizedek, whom it identifies with Shem son of Noah; but because he blessed Abram before he blessed God (Genesis 14:19–20), it was given to Abraham instead, and 110:4 is spoken to Abraham: a priest forever "because of the word of Melchizedek" (Bavli Nedarim 32b). The Dead Sea Scroll 11QMelchizedek pictures Melchizedek as a heavenly figure who frees captives and judges at the end of days; it does not quote Psalm 110, but it shows that Melchizedek was a figure of hope in the time of Jesus. Josephus explains his name as "righteous king" (Antiquities 1.180), and Philo makes him a picture of right reason.

a: The Lord stands at your right side;
t: Who is at whose right hand?
p: In 110:1 the king sits at God's right; in 110:5 "the Lord" is at the king's right, fighting for him.
b: Here the Hebrew has Adonai, the word for God. In battle a protector stood at a warrior's right, the side his shield did not cover (16:8; 121:5). So God, who seated the king at his right hand, now fights at the king's right. Some Christian readers took "the Lord" of 110:5–7 as the Messiah, the "lord" of 110:1, seated at God's right; others as God himself. The "day of his anger" links the psalm with the prophets' day of the LORD (Zephaniah 1:14–18) and with the rider who judges the nations in Revelation 19:11–21.

a: He shatters the head across the broad land.
p: Rosh is singular: a chief enemy, or heads in general. Some Christians heard Genesis 3:15.
b: Rosh is singular: "he shatters (the) head over a wide land". It may be collective, "heads", the leaders of many lands; or one chief enemy ruler; or "the head of a great land". Smashing an enemy's head is a stock picture of victory (68:21; Habakkuk 3:13). Christian readers connected it with the promise that the woman's offspring would strike the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15), though the Hebrew verbs differ. The line before, "the land is full of bodies", is the grim language of ancient victory hymns.
orig: מָחַץ רֹאשׁ עַל־אֶרֶץ רַבָּה (machats rosh 'al-erets rabbah)

a: On the way he drinks from a stream;
p: A puzzling ending: a warrior refreshed in the chase, a rite at a spring, or Christ's suffering and rising.
b: Three main readings. (1) A warrior chasing his enemies stops to drink and goes on refreshed, his head high (compare Gideon's men at the spring and Samson at En-hakkore, Judges 7:5–6; Judges 15:18–19). (2) A rite of the king's crowning: Solomon was made king at the Gihon spring below Jerusalem (1 Kings 1:33–45), and some think the new king drank from it. (3) Many church fathers read the stream "on the way" as the suffering Christ drank on his road, and the raised head as his resurrection and exaltation (Philippians 2:8–9).

a: Praise the LORD!
p: "Praise the LORD" stands outside the acrostic, as a heading for 111 and 112.
b: Hallelu-yah, "Praise Yah!", opens Psalms 111, 112 and 113 and closes 113, 115, 116 and 117. In 111 and 112 it stands outside the alphabet pattern, as a heading. Codex Vaticanus moves the "Hallelujah" at the end of several psalms to the start of the next one (see the variant at 113:9), so the placement of the word was not fixed in every copy. See the topic page on Hallelujah.

a: I will give the LORD thanks with all my heart,
p: Each half-line of Psalm 111 begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, 22 in all.
b: After the opening Hallelujah, Psalm 111 has 22 short lines, and each begins with the next of the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet: alef (odeh, "I will give thanks"), bet (besod, "in the close circle"), gimel (gedolim, "great"), dalet (derushim, "searched out"), and so on to shin and tav in 111:10. Verses 1–8 have two lines each, 111:9–10 three each. The form suggests completeness, praise "from A to Z", and may also have helped people learn the poem by heart. Psalm 112 has exactly the same plan. The chapter page lists the letters. See the topic page on acrostics.

a: in the close circle of the upright, and in the community.
p: Sod is a close, trusted circle; 'edah is the whole community. Thanks is given in both.
b: Sod is a circle of friends who share counsel or secrets (25:14; 55:14; Jeremiah 23:18). 'Edah is the whole community of Israel gathered (as in Exodus 12:3). The singer praises God both among close friends and before everyone, the private and public sides of worship. The bet line of the acrostic begins with besod.

a: searched out by everyone who takes pleasure in them.
t: A verse over a laboratory door
p: The Latin of this verse is carved over the doors of the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge.
b: Derushim means "sought out", "searched into": people who delight in God's works study them. When the Cavendish Laboratory for physics was built in Cambridge, England, in the 1870s, James Clerk Maxwell, its first professor, had the Latin of this verse carved over the door: Magna opera Domini exquisita in omnes voluntates eius. When the laboratory moved to new buildings in the 1970s, a research student proposed putting the verse over the entrance in English, in Coverdale's wording, and it was done. Many scientists have read the line as a blessing on the study of nature. In the psalm, God's "works" are chiefly his acts in Israel's history, as the next verses show.

a: He has set up a memorial of his wonders;
p: Israel remembers God's wonders by festivals such as Passover. Christians heard the Lord's Supper here.
b: "He has made a memorial for his wonders" probably means that God set up ways for his deeds to be remembered, above all the feasts. Passover is "a day of remembrance" (Exodus 12:14) and is kept so that "you will remember the day you came out of the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 16:3). Christians read the verse together with 111:5, "he has given food to those who fear him", and with Jesus' words "Do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24–25). Thomas Aquinas's office for the feast of Corpus Christi draws an antiphon at Vespers from 111:4–5.

a: gracious and compassionate is the LORD.
p: The pair comes from God's self-description on Sinai (Exodus 34:6). 112:4 gives it to the righteous person.
b: "Gracious and compassionate" (channun verachum) echoes the words God spoke of himself to Moses on Sinai: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious" (Exodus 34:6; compare Psalm 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). The twin psalm repeats the words of the righteous person (112:4): the one who fears God comes to look like him.

a: He hands out food to those who fear him;
p: Teref usually means prey torn by a lion. Here it is food God provides, perhaps the manna and quail.
b: Teref normally means prey that a beast tears (Genesis 49:9; Job 38:39); in Proverbs 31:15 it simply means food. Here it may recall the wilderness, when God fed Israel with manna and quail (Exodus 16:1–36; 105:40), since the next line speaks of the covenant. The tet line of the acrostic needed a word beginning with tet, and teref is one of few.

a: all his orders can be trusted.
p: Piqqudim, "orders" or "precepts", belongs to the language of Psalms 19 and 119.
b: Piqqudim are things someone has been charged to do, from a verb meaning to appoint or entrust. The word occurs only in the Psalms: here and in 103:18, 19:8 and twenty-one times in Psalm 119. The Plain renders it "orders" throughout. Here the God whose deeds are faithful gives orders that are "firm" (ne'emanim), reliable and lasting (111:8).

a: He sent his people redemption;
p: Zechariah's song at John the Baptist's birth opens with this line.
b: Pedut is a ransom or release, as from slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, begins his song: "Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, / for he has visited his people / and worked their redemption" (Luke 1:68), and goes on to speak of God remembering his holy covenant (Luke 1:72), as 111:9 does. The last line, "His name is holy and to be feared", is also echoed by Mary (Luke 1:49).

a: Wisdom starts with the fear of the LORD;
p: A motto of Israel's wisdom books, found also in Proverbs and Job.
b: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom" is the motto of Israel's wisdom teachers (Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10; Job 28:28; Sirach 1:14). Reshit can mean the start, the chief part or the first fruits. Here the line forms a bridge: Psalm 111 has praised God's works; Psalm 112 will describe the person who fears him (112:1). "All who do them" in the Hebrew means those who practice God's orders; the Greek has "who do it".

a: Happy is the person who fears the LORD,
p: Same alphabet plan, same length, and many of the same words, now said of the person who fears God.
b: Psalm 112 follows the same plan as Psalm 111: a Hallelujah, then 22 lines from alef to tav, eight verses of two lines and two of three. It takes up 111's words and applies them to the God-fearing person. God's righteousness "stands for all time" (111:3); so does the righteous person's (112:3, 9). God is "gracious and compassionate" (111:4); so is he (112:4). God's orders are "firm" (111:8); his heart is "firm" (112:7–8). It begins with ashrei-ish, "Happy is the person", the same words as Psalm 1:1, and the Plain renders them the same way. For the letters, see the chapter page.

a: There is wealth and plenty in his house,
p: The psalm promises the God-fearing wealth. Job, Ecclesiastes and other psalms know it does not always work out.
b: Like Psalm 1 and much of Proverbs, Psalm 112 promises the God-fearing person a blessed family, wealth and honor (Proverbs 3:9–10; Proverbs 22:4). Other books know the pattern does not always hold: Job loses everything, and 73:3–12 sees the wicked prosper. The psalm itself uses the wealth for others: the righteous man lends and gives freely to the poor (112:5, 9). Some readers take its promises as the way things tend to go under God's rule, not a guarantee for each life. Preachers of a "prosperity gospel" have read it more literally, and many other Christians reject that reading.

a: gracious, compassionate and righteous.
p: The three words have no subject. They may describe the righteous man, or God, the light that rises.
b: The Hebrew line has three adjectives and no noun. (1) They describe the upright man, using God's own words from 111:4 for him (most modern readers). (2) They describe God, who is the light rising in the dark (27:1; Isaiah 60:1–2); the singular forms fit God well. The Plain keeps the bare list, so either reading stays open.

a: Good comes to the person who is kind and lends;
p: In Israel a loan to the poor was charity, given without interest.
b: The law told Israelites to lend to a poor neighbor without charging interest and to forgive debts in the seventh year (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–11). So lending here is generosity, not business (compare 37:26; Proverbs 19:17, "Showing kindness to a poor man is a loan made to the LORD"). "He manages his affairs with justice" is literally "keeps his words in judgment": he is honest and fair in his dealings.

a: He has scattered, he has given to the needy.
p: Paul quotes this verse in its Greek form when he asks the Corinthians to give generously for Jerusalem.
b: Collecting money for the poor believers in Jerusalem, Paul tells the Corinthians that God loves a cheerful giver and can give them enough to share, "As it is written: 'He has scattered abroad. He has given to the poor. His righteousness remains forever.'" (2 Corinthians 9:9). The "he" of the psalm is the generous man, but Paul may be thinking of God too, since the next verse speaks of God supplying seed to the sower (2 Corinthians 9:10). "Scattered" is a sower's word: the gift is like seed that grows. In Jewish usage tsedaqah, "righteousness", came to mean charity, and this verse is part of that history.

a: his horn is raised high with honor
p: The horn is a picture of strength and dignity, taken from a bull or wild ox.
b: A horn is the pride and strength of a bull or wild ox (92:10; Deuteronomy 33:17). To have one's horn raised is to be strong and honored (75:10; 89:17; 1 Samuel 2:1). Zechariah's song calls the Messiah "a horn of rescue" (Luke 1:69).

a: The craving of the wicked will be lost.
p: The last words, "will be lost", are also the last words of Psalm 1.
b: The tav line begins ta'avat, "the craving", and the poem's last word is to'ved, "will be lost" or "will perish". Psalm 1 ends with the same verb: "but the road of the wicked will be lost" (1:6). Both poems begin "Happy is the person" (the same Hebrew), set the righteous and the wicked side by side, and end with the wicked fading out. The wicked man here "grinds his teeth" in rage and envy (35:16; 37:12), and he "melts away".

a: Praise the LORD!
p: Psalms 113–118 are sung at Passover and the great festivals. The rabbis called them the Egyptian Hallel.
b: Psalms 113–118 have long been sung as a set called the Hallel ("praise"), named later the "Egyptian Hallel" because 114:1 tells of the exodus from Egypt. The Mishnah says the Levites sang it while the Passover lambs were slaughtered (Mishnah Pesachim 5:7), and that at the Passover meal the family sings the first part (113, or 113–114) before the meal and finishes it after the last cup (Mishnah Pesachim 10:6–7). The Talmud lists the days in the year when the full Hallel is sung, including the eight days of Booths and of Hanukkah (Bavli Arakhin 10a). It is still sung in synagogues on festivals and the new moon. See the topic page on the Hallel.

a: Praise, servants of the LORD!
p: The Greek and Latin have "children" (paides, pueri), and Laudate pueri became a famous text for composers.
b: 'Avdei YHWH, "servants of the LORD", may mean the temple's priests and Levites (134:1; 135:1–2) or all Israel. The Greek has paides, which can mean both servants and children, and the Latin Laudate pueri Dominum, "Praise the Lord, you children". Under that Latin heading, Psalm 113 is sung at Vespers on Sundays and feasts, and composers such as Monteverdi, Vivaldi, Handel and Mozart set it to music.

a: Who is like the LORD our God,
p: The question was first asked in the song at the sea (Exodus 15:11).
b: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" (Exodus 15:11) is the question of Israel's first song after the exodus. Psalm 113 asks it again, and the next psalm sings of the exodus itself. The answer is that no one is: God sits higher than anyone, and yet bends lower than anyone to lift the poor (113:6–8). The name Michael means "Who is like God?"

a: who bends down low to look
p: God sits higher than the heavens and still bends down to see the earth.
b: "Who makes his seat high" and "who makes himself low to see" are a matched pair in the Hebrew: God's height is not distance. He is above the nations and the heavens (113:4) yet looks down at the heavens and the earth, and especially at the poor in the dust. Isaiah says the same: God lives "in the height and in holiness I dwell, and with the crushed and the lowly in spirit" (Isaiah 57:15). Christian writers saw this stooping fulfilled in the incarnation (Philippians 2:6–8).

a: He lifts the poor up out of the dust;
p: 113:7–8 is almost word for word from Hannah's song, and 113:9 tells Hannah's own story.
b: Verses 7–8 repeat 1 Samuel 2:8 almost exactly, and the Plain uses the site's wording from there. The garbage heap (ashpot) was the town dump, where beggars sat and the outcast slept (Lamentations 4:5; compare Job 2:8). Hannah sang these words when her son Samuel was born after years of barrenness, which is the subject of 113:9. Mary's song, sung when she was expecting Jesus, takes up the same themes: "He has pulled rulers down from thrones / and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52).

a: The barren woman of the house he seats
p: A childless wife given a family: Sarah, Rachel, Hannah, and in the prophets, Zion itself.
b: Childlessness was a great grief and shame for a woman in Israel. The stories of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson's mother and Hannah all tell of God giving a child to a woman who had none (Genesis 21:1–7; Genesis 30:22–23; Judges 13:2–3; 1 Samuel 1:1–20). Isaiah speaks to ruined Jerusalem as a barren woman who will have more children than she can count (Isaiah 54:1), and Paul applies Isaiah's words to the church (Galatians 4:27). Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist, belongs in the same line (Luke 1:7, 25). The verb "seats" matches 113:8: the God who seats beggars with princes seats the childless woman as mistress of a full house.
r: Genesis 21:1–7; Genesis 30:22–23; Judges 13:2–3; 1 Samuel 1:1–20; Isaiah 54:1; Galatians 4:27; Luke 1:7; Luke 1:25

a: from a people who babbled a foreign tongue,
p: Lo'ez means speaking a foreign tongue, babbling. The Greek has "a barbarian people".
b: Lo'ez occurs only here. In later Hebrew it means speaking a foreign language, and Rashi uses the word for the French glosses in his commentaries. The Greek renders it "a barbarian people", from the Greek word for those who do not speak Greek, which first meant people whose speech sounds like "bar-bar". Israel left a land where it did not understand the language, as Joseph's brothers once did (Genesis 42:23; compare Psalm 81:5).

a: When Israel went out from Egypt,
p: Dante used this verse to explain the four senses of Scripture.
b: In a letter attributed to him (Letter to Cangrande, 7), Dante explains the medieval "four senses" of Scripture by this verse. Literally it is the exodus under Moses; allegorically, our redemption by Christ; morally, the soul turned from sin to grace; and in the upward (anagogical) sense, the holy soul leaving this world for eternal glory. In the Purgatorio (2.46) the souls arriving at Purgatory sing In exitu Israel de Aegypto, the Latin of this verse. Jewish readers kept the exodus at the center: it is the reason for the Passover Hallel.

a: Judah became his holy place,
p: "His" holy place: the psalm does not name God until 114:7.
b: The psalm says "his holy place" and "his dominion" but does not say whose until 114:7, where the earth trembles "before the face of the Lord". Many readers think the delay is deliberate: the sea and the mountains react to someone unseen before the poem names him. Judah and Israel together stand for the whole people, God's sanctuary and kingdom (Exodus 19:6, "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation").

a: The sea saw and ran;
p: The Red Sea at the start of the journey and the Jordan at the end are joined in one picture.
b: The sea that split when Israel left Egypt (Exodus 14:21–22) and the Jordan that stopped when they entered Canaan (Joshua 3:13–17) stand side by side, the beginning and end of the exodus. The two crossings are joined in Joshua 4:23 as well. In Canaanite myth Sea (Yam) and River (Nahar) were one enemy of the storm god; in the psalm they are mere water that runs at the sight of Israel's God (compare 77:16; Habakkuk 3:8).

a: The mountains leapt like rams,
p: The mountains leap at Sinai, where the mountain shook when God came down.
b: When God came down on Sinai "the whole mountain shook violently" (Exodus 19:18; compare Psalm 68:8; Judges 5:5). Psalm 29:6 has Lebanon skipping like a calf. The comparison with rams and lambs is almost playful. In 114:5–6 the singer asks the sea and mountains what was wrong with them, and answers in 114:7.

a: Writhe, earth, before the face of the Lord,
p: Chul means to twist or writhe, as in labor or terror.
b: Chuli is a command: "writhe" or "tremble". The verb is used for a woman in labor (Isaiah 26:17) and for terror (96:9; 97:4). It answers the questions of 114:5–6: the whole earth, not just the sea and mountains, should shake before "Jacob's God".

a: who changes rock into a pond of water
p: God gave water from the rock at Rephidim and Kadesh. Paul says "the rock was Christ".
b: Twice in the wilderness God gave water from rock (Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 20:2–13; compare Psalm 78:15–16; 105:41). The psalm turns it into a picture of God's power over nature: hard flint becomes a spring. Paul writes that the Israelites "were drinking from a spiritual rock that went along with them, and that rock was the Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4).

a: Not to us, LORD, not to us,
p: The Greek, the Latin and many Hebrew manuscripts join 114 and 115 into one psalm.
b: In the Septuagint and the Vulgate, Psalms 114 and 115 are one psalm (Greek 113), and some Hebrew manuscripts also write them together. Most readers today see two poems: 114 a hymn about the exodus, 115 a prayer against idols with blessings for Israel. But the join makes sense: after the God of Jacob shook the earth (114:7), the nations ask, "Where is their God?" (115:2). From here on the Greek and Hebrew numbers are out of step by one, and Psalm 116 is split in two in the Greek.

a: Not to us, LORD, not to us,
p: The Latin opening, Non nobis, Domine, became a hymn of thanks for victory, and of the Knights Templar.
b: In Latin the verse begins Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam. It became a prayer of thanks after victory, giving the credit to God. In Shakespeare's Henry V, after Agincourt, the king orders "Non nobis" and the Te Deum to be sung (Act 4, Scene 8), and an Elizabethan setting of it is still sung. It was also the motto of the Knights Templar. It suits the psalm's point: if God's name is honored, it is because of his loyal love and faithfulness, not anything in his people.

a: "So where is their God?"
p: The nations' taunt in 79:10 and Joel 2:17. Israel's God has no image to point to.
b: The taunt appears in 42:3, 42:10, 79:10 and Joel 2:17. The neighbors could point to statues of their gods; Israel's temple had none, and after 587 BC Israel had no temple at all. The answer is that their God is in the heavens and does whatever he pleases (115:3); it is the nations' gods that are only objects. The Qumran scroll 4QPs-b (4Q84) lacks the little word na' ("So") in the taunt.

a: Their idols are silver and gold,
p: Silver and gold, made by hand: mouths that do not speak, eyes that do not see.
b: The satire of 115:4–8 is repeated almost word for word in 135:15–18, and Isaiah, Jeremiah and Habakkuk use the same kind of mockery (Isaiah 44:9–20; Jeremiah 10:3–5; Habakkuk 2:18–19). Babylonian priests performed a "washing of the mouth" and an "opening of the mouth" (mīs pî, pīt pî) on a new statue so that the god would come to live in it, and they would not have said they worshiped wood and metal. The psalm denies that anything happens: the mouth stays shut. The seven parts listed (mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands, feet, throats) are the senses and powers a living god should have.

a: The ones who make them will end up like them,
p: Idol makers become as deaf and blind as the idols. Many readers find a rule of all worship here.
b: The verse can be a wish ("May those who make them become like them") or a fact ("will become"). Either way, worship shapes the worshiper. 2 Kings 17:15 says Israel "went after vapor and became vapor", and Isaiah says the idol-maker cannot see what he holds (Isaiah 44:18–20; Isaiah 6:9–10). Gregory Beale has argued that this idea runs through the whole Bible: people become like what they revere, whether for ruin or, in Paul's words, for being "changed into the same image" of the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:18).

a: Israel, put your trust in the LORD!
p: Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD: perhaps a call and response in the temple.
b: Verses 9–11 address three groups, each answered with the same line, "He is their help and their shield", and 115:12–13 blesses the same three; 118:2–4 and 135:19–20 have similar lists. Israel is the whole people; the house of Aaron is the priests. "Those who fear the LORD" may be a summary of all the worshipers, or a separate group: foreigners who worshiped Israel's God, like the "God-fearers" of the book of Acts (Acts 10:2; Acts 13:16, 26). The change from "your" to "their" suggests a leader's call and a choir's or priest's answer.

a: The heavens are the LORD's own heavens,
p: God keeps the heavens and has given the earth to human beings, as in Genesis 1:28 and Psalm 8.
b: Literally, "The heavens are heavens for the LORD, but the earth he has given to the children of Adam." The line recalls God giving human beings rule over the earth (Genesis 1:28; 8:6). It also sets up the next verse: the earth, not the silent place of the dead, is where praise is sung.

a: The dead do not praise Yah,
p: The silent place is Sheol. Christians and Jews have read this line in different ways.
b: Dumah, "silence", is a name for the world of the dead (94:17). Like 6:5, 30:9 and 88:10–12, this verse gives a reason to praise now: the dead cannot. So "we" the living will bless Yah "from this moment on and for all time" (115:18). Both verses use Yah, the short form of God's name, which the Plain keeps as "Yah" (as in Exodus 15:2), while hallelu-yah stays "Praise the LORD!". The verse shows how most of the Old Testament pictures Sheol: a place of silence, not of worship. Later Jewish and Christian belief in resurrection and life with God after death (Daniel 12:2; Philippians 1:23) read the verse as about the body in the grave, or about those who die far from God. Some churches read it literally, as evidence that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection; see the chapter page.

a: I love, because the LORD hears
p: The Hebrew starts with "I love" and no object. Many versions move "the LORD" up.
b: The first word is ahavti, "I love". It has no object: the Hebrew goes straight on, "because the LORD hears". Most translations write "I love the LORD, because he hears", which smooths the line. The Plain keeps the bare "I love". Love for God is commanded (Deuteronomy 6:5), but it is seldom stated in the Psalms (18:1 is the other clear case). The Greek reads "I loved, for the Lord will listen".

a: Death's ropes closed around me;
p: The same line opens 18:4. The singer was seriously ill or in mortal danger.
b: The line repeats 18:4 (and 2 Samuel 22:5–6): death pictured as a hunter with ropes or snares. "The straits of Sheol", the world of the dead, have caught him. The cup of 116:13 and the vows of 116:14 suggest a sick person who has recovered and comes to the temple with a thank offering (116:17). The Greek has "dangers of Hades".

a: The LORD guards the simple;
p: Peta'im are the naive or inexperienced. Here they are people with no protection but God.
b: In Proverbs peti is the naive young person who believes anything and needs teaching (Proverbs 1:4; Proverbs 14:15). Here it means the open-hearted and defenseless, people who have no one else to rely on. The Greek has nēpia, "infants", and the LORD's decree "gives wisdom to the simple" in 19:7. Jesus thanks the Father for hiding things from the wise and showing them to infants (Matthew 11:25).

a: I kept trusting, even when I said,
p: Paul quotes the Greek of this verse in 2 Corinthians 4:13. The Hebrew is hard.
b: The Hebrew he'emanti ki adabber is hard: "I trusted, for I speak", "I kept faith even when I said", or "I believed when I spoke". The Greek, which starts a new psalm here (Greek 115), has "I believed, therefore I spoke". Paul quotes it: "We have the same spirit of faith as in what is written: 'I believed, and so I spoke.' We too believe, and so we too speak" (2 Corinthians 4:13). Like the psalmist, Paul has been near death (2 Corinthians 4:8–12) and trusts the God who raised Jesus. See the variant.

a: "Every human being lies."
p: Paul echoes the Greek in Romans 3:4: "Let God be true, and every human being a liar."
b: Said in alarm or haste (bechofzi, "in my panic"; Greek "in my ecstasy"), the line means that no human support could be trusted. Paul borrows it for a larger claim: "Let God be true, and every human being a liar" (Romans 3:4), before he quotes 51:4. Augustine read the Greek "ecstasy" as a moment of insight in which the singer saw the truth about human weakness.

a: I will raise the cup of rescue
p: A drink offering of thanks at the temple. The Roman Mass long used the verse at the priest's communion.
b: The "cup of rescues" (the noun is plural) was probably a cup of wine poured out or drunk at the thank offering (116:17; compare Numbers 28:7), raised in honor of the God who saved. At the Passover meal, Jewish families sing this psalm in the second half of the Hallel, after the meal. In the Tridentine Latin Mass the priest said this verse, Calicem salutaris accipiam, before drinking from the chalice, and Christians have long heard here the cup of the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 10:16). The Plain has "rescue" for yeshu'ah, as elsewhere on the site.

a: weighs heavily in the LORD's eyes.
p: Yaqar here means "costly" or "weighty": God does not lightly let his loyal ones die.
b: The KJV's "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints" is often read at funerals as if God valued or welcomed the death of the faithful. Yaqar means valuable, costly, weighty. In 72:14 "their blood is precious in his eyes" means God will not let it be shed cheaply. So here the death of God's loyal ones costs him too much to allow it lightly, which is why he freed the singer (116:16). Many Christians still find comfort in the verse at a death, in the sense that God cares how his people die.

a: your servant girl's son
p: A slave born in the house belonged there for life. The singer belongs to God from birth.
b: "Your servant, the son of your servant girl" (as in 86:16) is one who was born in the household, not bought, and so serves for life (Exodus 21:4; Genesis 14:14). "You have loosed my bonds" plays on it: God frees him from death's ropes (116:3), and he stays God's servant gladly. Mary calls herself "the Lord's servant girl" (Luke 1:38, 48).

a: All you nations, praise the LORD!
p: Paul quotes this verse among four texts showing that the nations will praise God with Israel.
b: Paul ends his long argument about Jews and Gentiles with a chain of quotations: 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, this verse and Isaiah 11:10 (Romans 15:9–12). All four have the nations praising Israel's God, and Paul uses them to say that Christ came to confirm the promises to Israel's ancestors "and so that the nations may glorify God for his mercy". The shortest psalm in the Bible thus becomes a key text for the mission to the Gentiles.

a: All you peoples, applaud him!
p: Psalm 117 is the shortest chapter and, by the KJV count, the middle chapter. The claim that 118:8 is the middle verse is mistaken.
b: In the 66 books and 1,189 chapters of the Protestant Bible, numbered as in the KJV, Psalm 117 is the 595th chapter, with 594 on either side, and it is also the shortest. The often-repeated claim that 118:8 is the middle verse is mistaken: the KJV has 31,102 verses, so there is no single middle verse, and the two middle verses are 103:1–2. A Catholic or Orthodox Bible with more books, or a Hebrew Bible with its own order, has a different middle. Chapter numbers were added in the 1200s and verse numbers in the 1500s, so none of this means anything in the text itself.

a: For his loyal love is mighty over us,
p: Gavar means to be strong or to prevail, as the flood waters "prevailed" over the earth.
b: Gavar 'al means to be mighty over, to prevail. It is used of the flood waters rising over the earth (Genesis 7:18–24) and in 103:11, where God's loyal love "stands strong over those who fear him" (the same Hebrew as "mighty over us" here). Here God's hesed rises over Israel like a flood, and the nations are to praise God for what he has done for Israel. The Greek has ekrataiōthē, "has been made strong".

a: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good;
p: They sang the hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives: the end of the Passover Hallel, Psalms 115–118.
b: Mark and Matthew say that after the Last Supper Jesus and his disciples "sang the hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives" (Mark 14:26; Matthew 26:30). If the meal was a Passover, as the first three Gospels present it, the hymn would have been the second part of the Hallel, ending with Psalm 118, completed over the fourth cup (Mishnah Pesachim 10:7). The Mishnah was written down about AD 200, so the practice in Jesus' day cannot be proven, but many scholars, Joachim Jeremias among them, think it likely. Read that way, the psalm's lines about the rejected stone, the cords of the festival offering, and "I will not die but live" were among the last words Jesus sang before his arrest.

a: Let Israel say,
p: Calls and responses, a procession to the gates, and a festival offering at the altar.
b: The psalm reads like the script of a festival procession. A leader calls three groups to answer "his loyal love is forever" (118:2–4; compare 115:9–11). A rescued king or leader tells his story (118:5–18), asks at the temple gates to be let in (118:19), and is answered (118:20). The crowd greets him (118:22–26), the priests bless him from the house of the LORD (118:26), and the procession, with branches, moves up to the altar (118:27). Many scholars link it with the Feast of Booths, when Psalm 118:25 was chanted around the altar (Mishnah Sukkah 4:5).

a: From the narrow place I called on Yah;
p: Yah is the short form of God's name. The Plain keeps it as "Yah", as in Exodus 15:2, which 118:14 quotes.
b: Yah is a short form of the divine name YHWH, used in poetry and in "Hallelu-yah". It comes six times in Psalm 118 (118:5 twice, 14, 17, 18, 19). The Plain keeps "Yah" wherever it stands alone, as in the site's Exodus 15:2, which 118:14 quotes word for word; it already came in 115:17–18. In hallelu-yah it is "Praise the LORD!". "The narrow place" (metsar) and "the open" (merchav, broad space) are the Hebrew pictures of trouble and rescue (see the note on 107:6).

a: What can a human being do to me?
p: Hebrews quotes the Greek of this verse as a reason to live without greed or fear.
b: "The Lord is a helper to me; I will not be afraid. What will a human being do to me?" (Hebrews 13:6). Hebrews joins it to God's promise never to leave or abandon his people (Deuteronomy 31:6) as a reason to be content and not love money (Hebrews 13:5). 56:11 has nearly the same line, and the Plain uses that wording here. Romans 8:31, "If God is for us, who is against us?", may also echo it.

a: Sheltering in the LORD is better
p: A wisdom saying: trusting God is better than trusting even the great.
b: "Better... than" is the form of a wisdom saying (Proverbs 15:16–17). Verses 8–9 contrast refuge in God with trust in human beings and in princes, the powerful patrons people hoped would protect them (146:3; Jeremiah 17:5–7). Both Qumran scrolls that have the verse, 4QPs-b and 11QPs-a, read "trust" (bateach) in the first half instead of "take shelter" (see the variant). The popular claim that 118:8 is the middle verse of the Bible is mistaken (see the note on Psalm 117).

a: in the LORD's name I cut them down.
p: The verb amil is odd. Most take it as "cut off"; some as "circumcise"; the Greek has "I warded them off".
b: Amilam comes from mul, which usually means "circumcise". Most take it here as "cut off" or "cut down", from a second verb with the same letters. A few connect it with circumcision, as when David brought Philistine foreskins to Saul (1 Samuel 18:25–27). The Greek has "I warded them off". The line is repeated three times (118:10–12) with growing force: the nations surround him like bees, but he wins "in the LORD's name".

a: They swarmed around me like bees;
p: A swarm that cannot be beaten off, and a brush fire that flares and dies at once.
b: Bees chasing an enemy are a picture of an army in Deuteronomy 1:44 and Isaiah 7:18. Dry thornbushes catch fire at once, crackle loudly and burn out fast (Ecclesiastes 7:6). The Hebrew says the enemies "flickered out" like such a fire; the Greek says they "blazed up" like it. Either way, the danger is fierce and short.

a: My strength and my song is Yah,
p: This verse quotes Exodus 15:2 word for word, and Isaiah 12:2 quotes it too.
b: "My strength and my song is Yah, and he has become my rescue" is the second line of the song Moses and Israel sang at the sea (Exodus 15:2); Isaiah 12:2 quotes it as well. The psalm goes on with more of that song's language: "the right hand of the LORD" doing mighty deeds (118:15–16; Exodus 15:6, 12). The Hallel that began with the exodus in Psalm 114 ends with the singer's own rescue told in the words of the first rescue. "Song" (zimrat) may also mean "strength" or "protection".

a: I will not die, for I will live
p: Martin Luther called Psalm 118 "my own psalm" and wrote 118:17 on his study wall.
b: In 1530, while he waited at Coburg Castle during the Diet of Augsburg, Martin Luther wrote a long exposition of Psalm 118 (the Confitemini, from the Latin of 118:1), calling it "my own beloved psalm" which had helped him out of many troubles. He wrote 118:17 on his wall in Latin, with a musical setting: Non moriar sed vivam, et narrabo opera Domini. Christians have also read the verse as a word of Christ's resurrection.

a: Yah has trained me with hard discipline,
p: God's discipline is the training of a father, not destruction.
b: Yasar is to train or discipline, as a father does a son (Proverbs 3:11–12; Deuteronomy 8:5). The doubled verb, "he has disciplined me, disciplined", stresses how hard it was, but it stops short of death. Hebrews 12:5–11 quotes Proverbs on the same theme, and Paul writes, "We are dying, and look, we live on. We are punished, and yet not put to death" (2 Corinthians 6:9).

a: Open the gates of righteousness for me;
p: The singer asks to enter the temple, and the gatekeepers answer that only the righteous may go in.
b: "Gates of righteousness" are the temple gates, so called because only the righteous may enter. The question "Who may go up?" was asked at the gates and answered by the priests (15:1–5; 24:3–6). Here the answer is "This is the gate that belongs to the LORD; through it the righteous will enter" (118:20). Jesus says, "I am the door. Whoever goes in through me will be rescued" (John 10:9), and 118:20 is sometimes printed beside it.

a: A stone that the builders threw out
p: A stone the builders judged unfit becomes the most important stone in the building.
b: Builders looked over cut stones and threw out the ones they thought flawed. The one rejected here becomes "the head of the corner": either the cornerstone at the base, which squares the walls, or a capstone or keystone at the top. In the psalm the stone is probably the rescued king or leader, written off by the nations (118:10–13) and now honored, or Israel itself, despised and then restored. Isaiah speaks of God laying a precious cornerstone in Zion (Isaiah 28:16), and Zechariah of a capstone set with shouts of "Grace!" (Zechariah 4:7).

a: has become the head of the corner
p: Jesus quotes 118:22–23 after the parable of the tenants; Peter, Paul and 1 Peter apply it to him.
b: After telling how tenants of a vineyard killed the owner's son, Jesus asks, "Have you not read this scripture: 'A stone that the builders threw out has become the head of the corner; from the Lord this came about, and in our eyes it is a marvel'?" (Mark 12:10–11; Matthew 21:42; Luke 20:17). The leaders realize he told the parable against them (Mark 12:12). Peter tells the council that Jesus is "the stone that you, the builders, treated as nothing" (Acts 4:11). 1 Peter 2:4–8 joins this verse with Isaiah 28:16 and Isaiah 8:14, and Ephesians 2:20 calls Christ the cornerstone of the church. There may be a pun in Hebrew between even, "stone", and ben, "son".
r: Mark 12:1–12; Matthew 21:33–46; Luke 20:9–19; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Ephesians 2:20; Isaiah 8:14; Isaiah 28:16

a: A stone that the builders threw out
p: The Targum makes the stone the boy David; Rashi reads it as Israel among the nations.
b: The Aramaic Targum turns the stone of 118:22 into a boy whom the builders rejected, who was among the sons of Jesse and was found worthy to be king and ruler: that is, David, the youngest son passed over until Samuel anointed him (1 Samuel 16:6–13). Rashi takes the stone as Israel, scorned among the nations and destined to be honored. Some later Jewish interpreters applied it to the Messiah. Like the Christian reading, these see a reversal planned by God: "From the LORD this came about" (118:23).

a: This is the day the LORD has acted;
p: The Hebrew says "This is the day the LORD has made" or "has acted": the day of this rescue, not every day.
b: Zeh hayyom 'asah YHWH can be read "This is the day the LORD has made" (KJV), a line often used to greet any day as God's gift. In context the "day" is the day of this rescue, the day the rejected stone was honored. 'Asah often means "act" or "do" (as in 22:31; 37:5). The Plain has "has acted" to show this. The Latin, Haec dies quam fecit Dominus, is sung throughout Easter week, so Christians hear the day of resurrection in it.

a: LORD, please, save us now!
p: Hoshi'ah na, "save, please", became "Hosanna", the shout of the crowds when Jesus entered Jerusalem.
b: Hoshi'ah na means "Save, please!"; the Hebrew has no "us", which the Plain adds because the people are praying for themselves. In the temple at the Feast of Booths, priests walked around the altar every day with willow branches chanting this verse (Mishnah Sukkah 4:5), and the willow bundles and the seventh day itself came to be called "Hoshana". By Jesus' time the plea had become a shout of praise: when Jesus rode into Jerusalem, the crowds waved branches and cried "Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name" (Mark 11:9–10; Matthew 21:9; John 12:13). The word is still sung in the Christian Sanctus, "Hosanna in the highest", and in Jewish prayers at Booths.

a: Blessed is the one who comes in the LORD's name!
p: Pilgrims were greeted this way at the temple. The Gospels apply it to Jesus.
b: In the psalm the priests bless the one who arrives at the temple, perhaps the king leading the procession or any pilgrim, with "in the LORD's name" going with "blessed". "We bless you, all of you" is plural, a greeting to the whole crowd. In the Gospels the line greets Jesus as he enters Jerusalem (Mark 11:9; Luke 19:38, which adds "the king"; John 12:13, "the king of Israel"). John the Baptist asks whether Jesus is "the Coming One" (Matthew 11:3). Jesus tells Jerusalem it will not see him again until it says "Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name" (Matthew 23:39; Luke 13:35). The Benedictus in the Christian Mass joins this line to "Hosanna".
r: Mark 11:9; Luke 19:38; John 12:13; Matthew 11:3; Matthew 23:39; Luke 13:35

a: Tie the festival offering with cords
p: Chag can mean the festival or its sacrifice. The line may also mean "join the dance with branches".
b: Isru chag ba'avotim literally says "bind the festival with cords (or branches)". (1) Chag can mean the festival offering (Exodus 23:18; Malachi 2:3), tied with ropes until the moment of sacrifice. (2) Or chag is the festival procession, and 'avotim are leafy branches, as in Ezekiel 19:11 ("Her stature rose above the leafy boughs"), like the Booths procession. The Greek reads "Arrange a festival with thick boughs". Jewish tradition named the day after each pilgrimage festival Isru Chag after this verse. Christian readers have heard the binding of Jesus, the sacrifice, in the first reading.

a: The LORD is God, and he gave us light.
p: The Greek, "God is the Lord and has appeared to us", is sung at every Orthodox Matins.
b: The Greek reads Theos kyrios kai epephanen hēmin, "God is the Lord, and he has appeared to us", the same verb as in the word Epiphany. In Byzantine morning prayer (Matins), "God is the Lord and has appeared to us; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord" (118:27, 26) is sung with verses of this psalm almost every day. In the Hebrew, "he gave us light" recalls the priestly blessing: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you" (Numbers 6:25).
